title: Google Dorking: Asking the Right Questions
introduction: A normal Google search finds what Google thinks is most relevant to your query. A Google Dork finds what Google has indexed that matches very specific structural criteria — not 'find me pages about login pages' but 'find me actual login pages on this exact domain.' The difference is the difference between a general question and a surgical query. Both use the same search bar.

sections.heading: The core operators (and what each one reveals)
sections.content:
Google search operators are special commands that modify how Google searches its index. Learning eight of them covers 90% of professional reconnaissance use.

---

**site:** — Limit results to one domain.
Example: site:meridian-financial.com
Shows everything Google has indexed for that domain. The result count tells you how large the indexed footprint is. Use this first on every target.

---

**filetype:** — Find specific file types.
Example: site:meridian-financial.com filetype:pdf
Finds indexed PDF files. Common targets: pdf (documents), xlsx (spreadsheets), docx (Word documents), txt (plain text, often configuration or notes), sql (database files — rare but critical when found), pptx (presentations), env (environment configuration — often contains credentials).

---

**intitle:** — Find pages where the title contains specific text.
Example: intitle:"index of"
The most common directory listing dork. Web servers with directory listing enabled generate a page with "Index of /" in the title. intitle:"index of" site:target.com finds any open directory on their domain.

---

**inurl:** — Find pages where the URL contains specific text.
Example: site:meridian-financial.com inurl:admin
Finds URLs containing 'admin' on the target domain. Also useful: inurl:login, inurl:portal, inurl:manager, inurl:phpmyadmin, inurl:wp-admin (WordPress), inurl:config.

---

**intext:** — Find pages containing specific text in the body.
Example: site:meridian-financial.com intext:"confidential"
Finds pages or documents where 'confidential' appears in the content. Also: intext:"internal use only", intext:"password", intext:"username", intext:"BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY" (this one finds exposed private keys).

---

**cache:** — View Google's cached copy of a page.
Example: cache:meridian-financial.com/old-portal
Retrieves the last version Google cached. Useful when a page has been taken down — Google's cached copy may still show what was there. Note: Google is removing the cache: operator in some regions.

---

**"exact phrase"** — Require an exact phrase in results.
Example: "meridian financial" filetype:xlsx
Searches across the entire web for spreadsheets mentioning 'meridian financial' — finds documents on third-party sites (regulators, partners, news sites) that contain that organisation's data.

---

**- (minus)** — Exclude terms from results.
Example: site:meridian-financial.com -www
Excludes results from the www subdomain — focuses the search on other subdomains.

sections.heading: Combining operators: how professionals actually search
sections.content:
Individual operators are useful. Combinations are powerful. Professional Google Dork queries chain operators together.

**Finding sensitive documents:**
site:target.com filetype:pdf intitle:confidential
site:target.com filetype:xlsx
site:target.com filetype:docx "internal use only"
site:target.com filetype:env
site:target.com filetype:sql

**Finding exposed directories:**
site:target.com intitle:"index of"
site:target.com intitle:"index of" inurl:backup
site:target.com intitle:"index of" inurl:upload

**Finding login portals:**
site:target.com inurl:admin
site:target.com inurl:login
site:target.com inurl:portal
site:target.com inurl:wp-admin (WordPress admin)
site:target.com inurl:phpmyadmin

**Finding configuration files:**
site:target.com filetype:conf
site:target.com filetype:cfg
site:target.com filetype:ini
site:target.com filetype:log
site:target.com ext:env

**Finding information about the organisation across the web:**
"target company name" filetype:xlsx (spreadsheets anywhere mentioning them)
"target company name" password (mentions of passwords on any indexed page)
"target company name" "internal" filetype:pdf

Professional practice: Start with site:target.com alone to understand the total indexed footprint. Then systematically narrow with filetype:, inurl:, and intitle: operators. Document every finding before moving to the next query.

callout.title: The Google Hacking Database (GHDB)
callout.content: exploit-db.com/google-hacking-database contains over 4,000 curated Google Dork queries categorised by what they find: sensitive files, authentication bypass opportunities, network information, server configuration errors, and more. Professional penetration testers reference the GHDB to ensure they have not missed a common exposure pattern on their target. It is searchable by category and keyword.

sections.heading: robots.txt and sitemap.xml: the maps organisations publish to crawlers
sections.content:
Every well-configured website has two files at its root that exist specifically to communicate structure to search engine crawlers. Both are publicly readable. Both are gold for reconnaissance.

**robots.txt** — Tells crawlers which paths NOT to visit.
Located at: target.com/robots.txt

A typical robots.txt might read:
User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/
Disallow: /api/v1/
Disallow: /staff-only/
Disallow: /backup/
Sitemap: https://target.com/sitemap.xml

What this tells a professional: the organisation has a path called /admin/, a path called /api/v1/, a staff portal, and a backup directory. These are the paths they specifically did NOT want search engines to index — which means they are the most sensitive paths on the site. Read robots.txt immediately. Every disallowed path gets visited directly.

Critical point: robots.txt does NOT restrict access. It requests that cooperative crawlers skip certain paths. It has no enforcement mechanism. Any visitor — including a penetration tester — can visit /admin/ directly, robots.txt or not.

**sitemap.xml** — Tells crawlers which paths the site WANTS indexed.
Located at: target.com/sitemap.xml (or referenced from robots.txt)

A sitemap lists every URL the organisation considers part of their public website. This is the complete official map of intended public content — which is useful as a baseline. Any URL discovered elsewhere that is NOT in the sitemap is either intentionally private or accidentally exposed.

Professional use: Download both files at the start of every web reconnaissance session. robots.txt reveals sensitive paths. sitemap.xml establishes the intended public footprint baseline.

callout.title: robots.txt is a list of targets, not a protection
callout.content: Security professionals say: 'robots.txt is where the secrets are kept.' This is because organisations tend to list their most sensitive internal paths in robots.txt Disallow directives. The paths are not protected — they are announced. A tester who skips reading robots.txt may miss the admin path the organisation was specifically trying to hide from indexing.

sections.heading: Cached pages: the internet never forgets
sections.content:
Google does not just index pages — it stores copies. When Googlebot visits a page, it downloads and stores a snapshot. This snapshot is the 'cached' version. You can see it by clicking 'Cached' in Google results (where available) or by using the cache: operator.

Why this matters in reconnaissance:

**Deleted pages still exist in cache.** If an organisation published a sensitive page and then removed it, Google's cache may still contain the content. The cache persists for days to weeks after a page is removed.

**Cache shows the page as it was on the last crawl.** If a page was accessible without authentication at some point in the past — even if it now requires login — the cached version shows what was visible then.

**The Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) goes further.** The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine stores historical snapshots of websites dating back to the late 1990s. It often contains: old website versions revealing infrastructure that was later hidden, documents that were published and removed, and historical configurations. For any organisation that has been online for more than a few years, the Wayback Machine is a primary reconnaissance source.

Cached pages show what was — which is often different from what the organisation wants you to see now.

callout.title: Wayback Machine in professional practice
callout.content: web.archive.org — Enter any domain and see historical snapshots. Professionals use it to find: old admin panel paths that have since been renamed but may still work, employee names from 'About Us' pages that have been updated, historical subdomain structures, and old technology stack information from source code or headers. An organisation that switched platforms in 2022 may still have the old platform's URLs still responding.

keyTerms.definition: A search query using Google's advanced operators to find specific types of content in the Google index. Named after Johnny Long's technique documented in the Google Hacking Database.
Limits Google search results to a specific domain. site:company.com returns only pages Google has indexed from that domain.
Filters results to a specific file format. site:company.com filetype:pdf returns only PDFs Google has indexed from that domain.
Filters results where the page title contains the specified text. intitle:"index of" finds directory listing pages.
Filters results where the URL contains the specified text. inurl:admin finds pages with 'admin' in the URL.
A text file at a website's root that requests search engine crawlers skip certain paths. Not a security control — paths listed as Disallow are still publicly accessible.
A file listing all URLs the organisation intends to be publicly indexed. The official map of intended public content — useful as a baseline to identify unintended exposures.
A snapshot of a web page stored by Google at the time of its last crawl. May contain content that has since been removed from the live site.
